Violation of Indus Water Treaty 
2303. DR. AKHILESH DAS:  
 SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA:  
 SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the second round of Secretary level talks on 
Baglihar with Pakistan have broken down; 
(b) what are the technical issues raised by Pakistan during the above 
meeting; 
(c) whether it is a fact that India is really following  the Indus Water 
Treaty of 1960 and preparing design for the above 450 mw project; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) During the second meeting 
between India and Pakistan at Secretary level held at New Delhi in January, 
2005, there appeared to be possibility of convergence on some of the 
technical issues raised by Pakistan and accordingly, the Indian Secretary 
requested for further discussions for one week between technical experts 
of the two countries afterwhich the Secretary level meeting could resume. 
207 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
Pakistan agreed to this suggestion provided India agrees to first suspend the work 
of project, which is not provided for in the Treaty and was not acceptable to 
us. 
(b) During the meeting, Secretary (Water & Power), Government of 
Pakistan tabled a list of following 6 technical issues: 
(i) Why not weir at low-level consistent with the Treaty? 
(ii) Calculations of Pondage. Calculation of Firm Power. Consistency with 
the Treaty. 
(iii) Calculations for fixing level of intake consistent with the Treaty. 
(iv) Why not ungated spillway? Why gates necessary? "If necessary," are 
these at highest level? Calculations consistent with Treaty needed. 
(v) Calculations and justification of Free Board in light of the Treaty 
provisions. 
(vi) Low-level tunnel—Plugging of tunnel—When?—After testing or 
commissioning—Inspection. ' 
(c) and (d) The Indus Water Treaty between India and Pakistan is being 
implemented in letter and spirit by the Government of India. India is of the 
view that the design of the Project is in strict conformity with the provisions 
of the Treaty and does not contravene t he criteria (a), (c), (e) & (f) of 
Paragraph 8 of Annexure D to the Treaty, as allegedly Pakistan, in light 
of the following: 
• There being no breast walls in the spillways and the top of the chute 
spillway gates being flush with the Full Pondage Level (FPL), there is no 
scope of artificial raising of water level above the FPL. 
• Pondage is based on minimum mean discharge of the river at the site 
(125.89 cumecs) in order to meet daily and weekly load fluctuations 
within the limitations as stipulated in the Treaty. 
• Ungated Spillway is not techno-economically viable from the 
considerations of topography, submergence, energy dissipation, reservoir 
siltation etc. The deep seated sluice spillways which serve the dual function 
of silt exclusion & flood discharge, are in line with the prevailing practice in 
respect of rivers with high silt load. The 
208 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
crest of the sluice spillway has been fixed from considerations of effective 
silt flushing based on prevalent practices and model studies. The model 
studies have, in fact, indicated still deeper seating of the spillways. 
• The sill of high level intake has been located below the dead storage level to 
ensure uninterrupted flow without formation of vortices and ingress of air 
into the tunnel. The water seal has been based on various established 
national and international practices/formulae. The hydraulic model studies 
indicate for further increasing the water seal.

Information system for water related data 
2308. DR. K. KASTURIRANGAN: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether as per the National Water Resources Policy 2002, 
Government have proposed to establish an information system for water 
related data at State/National level; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether progress in this regard is satisfactory; and 
(d) if so, what are the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) Yes, 
Sir. The provisions in the National Water Policy, 2002 in respect of 
Information System are as under: 
"2.1 A well developed information system, for water related data in 
its entirety, at the National/State level, is a prime requisite for resource 
planning. A standardised national information system should be 
established with a network of data banks and data bases, integrating 
and strengthening the existing Central and State level agencies and 
improving the quality of data and the processing capabilities. 
2.2 Standards for coding, classification, processing of data and 
methods/procedures for its collection should be adopted. Advances 
in information technology must be introduced to create a modern 
information system promoting free exchange of data among various 
agencies. Special efforts should be made to develop and continuously 
upgrade technological capability to collect, process and disseminate 
reliable data in the desired time frame. 
2.3 Apart from the data regarding water availability and actual water 
use, the system should also include comprehensive and reliable 
projections of future demands of water for diverse purposes." 
Under Hydrology Project completed in December 2003, a Hydrological 
Information System (HIS) has been established in 9 States and 6 Central 
agencies. The information system includes the facilities for data collection, 
processing, storage, retrieval and listing of data availability in data centres.

Under the Hydrology Project Phase-ll (HP-II), extension of HIS to 4 new

Inclusion of river erosion in Natural Calamity Management Act 
2315. SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the issue of river erosion is yet to be included 
in the National Calamity Management Act, 2000; 
(b) if so, whether the erosion by the river Brahmaputra and its tributaries 
has turned into a serious problem for Assam; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the Central Government has still not 
given due attention to the problem and even it was not included in the list 
of calamities; and 
222 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, the details thereof, and the steps being taken to control the 
erosion of river Brahmaputra and its tributaries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) No 
Act by the name of "National Calamity Management Act, 2000" has been 
enacted or introduced in the Parliament. Flood Management including 
erosion control being a State subject, investigation, planning and 
implementation of Flood Management and erosion control Schemes are 
within the purview of the State Government. The Central Government renders 
assistance, which are technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. 
Gpvernment of India has set up Brahmaputra Board under an act of 
Parliament. The responsibility of the Board inter alia includes preparation 
of Master Plan to control bank er osion in the Brahmaputra and Barak 
Valleys. 25 Master Plans including that of Brahmaputra have so far been 
prepared and sent to the State Go vernments for implementation. The 
Government of India had also been extending Central Loan Assistance to 
the State Government of Assam from 1974-75 to 1999-2000. An amount of 
Rs. 390.94 crore was released to the State Government of Assam as loan 
and Rs. 10.09 crore as Grant-in-Aid till March 2000. In addition an amount 
of Rs. 163.95 crore also provided to Assam since 1998-99 till date for 
taking up critical anti erosion and flood control schemes. 
Further, Brahmaputra Board has completed anti erosion schemes worth 
Rs. 21.91 crore in Assam and schemes at an estimated cost of Rs. 45.18 
crore are further proposed to be taken up during Tenth Plan. 
During the year 2004-05 the Government of India has approved the 
scheme, "Critical flood control and anti erosion scheme in Brahmaputra 
and Barak valley" under state sector with estimated cost of Rs. 150.00 
crore as the share of Central Government (90% grant and 10% loan), for 
North Eastern States including Assam. 
Recognizing the importance of the flood management and erosion 
control, the Government of India also constituted a High Level Task Force 
to look into the problems of Assam and other flood prone States which 
has brought the issues in focus and has suggested various measures for 
effective flood management and erosion control.

Need to declare Minimum Support Price For Guar, Moth, 
Coriander, Cumin, Methi And Isabgol Crops In Rajasthan 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, Rajasthan is the major 
bajra producing State in the country. It is grown in about 44 lakh hectares. 
Government of India has declared MSP of Rs. 515/- per quintal for bajra for 
kharif 2004 season which is insufficient. It should be, at least, Rs. 530/-
per quintal, as requested by the State Government. Further, FCI does not 
procure coarse-grain directly; it relies on States which have severely limited 
resources and it takes longer period to settle their claims with the 
Government. The Government is requested to issue necessary directions 
to FCI to purchase coarse-grain directly. 
(MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair) 
Rajasthan is also a leading State in the production of guar, moth, 
coriander and cumin. The State produces about 80 per cent of the total 
produce of guar in the country, while State is ranked number one in the 
production of moth. The total area covered under these crops is 
approximately four lakh hectares. Approximately, four million farm families 
depend for their livelihood on these crops. Isabgol and methi are also 
important medicinal/spice crops of Rajasthan. The Government has so far 
not declared MSP for these crops. The State Government has also requested 
to the Government of India to declare MSP for isabgol and methi apart 
from guar, moth, dhania and jeera. I would like to request the Central 
Government to immediately declare MSP for guar, moth, coriander, cumin, 
methi and isabgol, as these are important crops of Rajasthan but have not 
ben covered under MSP so far.

MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, a progressive civil society is

This is true with India also. We are a progressive democracy with secular

In a civil society the litigant should have easy, quick and inexpensive

Concern over the misconduct of Soldiers while travelling in 
trains in the Country 
SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI (Madhya Pradesh): Sir, they glittered in a 
special version of glory on parade. Out there on the "front", they have 
always done the nation proud. That is what makes it so painful, so difficult 
to believe. Members of that distinguished fraternity throwing people out of 
a railway carriage which they wanted for themselves. Even if they were 
unaware of another train thundering down the adjacent track, what those 
jawans did defies description. Their disgraceful misconduct, it is true, does 
not obliterate the more shining facets of our soldiers' showing. Yet the 
converse is equally true. 
It would now be vital that senior officers accept the reality that something 
is wrong; the system is breaking down. No longer can they afford to try 
and downplay such incidents by pointing to a handful of men from a one-
million-strong organisation being involved in unsavoury events that are blown 
out of proportion by sensation-seeking media. They have to understand 
240 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
that even a tiny leak will eventually succeed in draining a reservoir; in the 
present context, the reservoir of admiration, goodwill and support that has 
added to the weight of the punch the soldier throws. 
This was by no means a rare incident. Soldiers objecting, often violently, 
to passengers taking up position in unreserved railway carriages is 
common. What many of them do not appreciate is that civilians too have 
pressing reasons to travel, and that the discomfort (to put it mildly) resulting 
from too many ticket-holders and limited accommodation is across the 
board. Trying to muscle their way to stretch their legs is not acceptable. 
This is the message that the "bras" must send out. Soldiers on leave 
must be as disciplined as when they are on parade.

Demand for change of site of the second Airport in Pune in 
Maharashtra 
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSH I (Maharashtra): Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir, the Government of India has decided to construct a new 
international airport for Pune in the vicinity of the township of Chakan. 
The proposed construction of the said airport involves displacement of a large 
number of villagers from the Ambethan village, including a whole community of 
farmers who have already been once displaced on account of the construction of 
the Pawana Dam only 30 years back. 
The site of the proposed airport is in close vicinity of some sacred and historic 
monuments associated with the great saint Tukaram and requires cutting down of 
large tracts of forests on the western slopes of Sahyadris. The site chosen for the 
airport is such as to involve massive earthwork for levelling hills and filling up the 
ravines. The plot of land of about 7000 hectares, which was earmarked for 
acquisition for the development of an industrial estate (Chakan Phase-l l), which 
was denotified later on, remains unused till date. 
The farmers of the land, previously earmarked for acquisition, are willing to make 
that land available for the construction of the airport. The site now proposed for the 
airport includes some prime agricultural land that has

construction of the proposed site involves the displacement of the national

construction of a second airport for Pune, at Chakan, and choose a new site that

PROF. M.M. AGARWAL (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, "Health for All" is the slogan of 
the Central Government. People belonging to the lower and middle classes in the 
country are mainly dependent on the Government hospitals, but they are 
disappointed with the poor qualities of services rendered by them. The Central 
Government hospitals are over-crowded for want of medical facilities. Common' 
problems such as lack of adequate beds, over-crowding in both OPDs and 
Emergencies, lack of doctors and staff, lack of cleanliness and proper 
maintenance, shortage of essential medicines etc. are being faced by the 
people in the Government hospitals. The poor and common people come to Delhi for 
treatment in the Government hospitals. Due to influx of patients from various parts 
of the country, the hospitals are under constant pressure and admit patients more 
than their capacity/That is why, these days, two to three patients have to share 
a bed in many wards in the hospitals. Patients come to these hospitals for 
medical treatment, but they are returned back and referred to other 
Government/MCD/NDMC hospitals on the ground that they have neither 
adequate place for admission nor sufficient doctors/staff and medical facilities. 
Sir, there is a phenomenal increase in the number of patients with no 
corresponding increase in the number of existing beds and other infrastructural 
facilities. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Central Government that in view of the present 
deteriorating scenario of these hospi tals, it should immediately take 
necessary steps for improvement and expansion of medical facilities so that the 
poor people in the country can take better treatment,

Need to take immediate action to prevent subversion of the P.g. 
regulations, 2000 of the Medical Council of India 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Sir, my Special Mention 
concerns the Ministry of Health's directive to the Medical Council of India 
asking it to formulate provisions to designate all the "Non-Teaching 
Specialists" as Professors or Assist ant Professors, etc. Now, the MCI 
has made certain recommendations which would seriously jeopardize the 
basic character and quality of medical education in our country by altering 
the due process of selection. 
As per the existing MCI norms, a duly constituted Selection Committee 
of the UPSC or University must se lect a medical college teacher from 
among the most eligible candidates fulfilling the minimum MCI norms, 
who clear the all India open selection process, after having cleared a fitness-
to-teach bar. But now the selection process based on sheer merit and 
aptitude to teach is being replaced by a process based on the number of 
years of non-teaching service in any non-teaching hospital so that any 
non-teaching specialist with 18 year s of non-teaching experience will 
automatically become a professor without having to pass the UPSC and 
MCI mediated All India Selection Test for the Medical College Teaching 
Sub-Cadre. 
Sir, this move of the Ministry of Health is in violation of the MCl's own 
basic constitution, which serves as the custodian of the highest standards 
of medical education. It will result in the destruction of basic quality control 
benchmarks for medical faculty and education across the country. It calls 
for attention and urgent immediate action to prevent the subversion of the 
PG Regulations, 2000 of the MCI. Thank you.

SHRIMANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Thank you very much, Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir. I will certainly abide by your ruling. I will try. Sir, I am quite 
anxious to say—you will certainly appreciate, you are a very senior Member in 
this House-that since the last five years, every year, I find that whenever there is 
not other business— Government Business or other businesses— the slot is filled 
in by this sort of a discussion. Perhaps this is the fifth time that I have stood on my 
legs to discuss about farmers' suicide. Sir, why I say so? Of course, I must 
express my gratitude to the hon. Members, around 15 per cent of the Members 
are present in this House. I am very much gratified that they are kindly listening 
to the very important discussion which concerns the nation, which concerns all 
the Legisatures that the farmers are committing suicide in numbers due to 
pauperisation, continuous pauperisation. Sir, from this, I must say there are two 
sorts of treatment. One is called palliative treatment in which mostly doctors 
who do not understand the exact root of the disease, they will go for palliative 
treatment and, Sir, good doctors will go for curative treatment. They will not treat 
the symptoms, they will treat the root  cause of the disease. And, Sir, 
unfortunately, we talk about palliative treatment only. We don't talk about 
curative treatment. We don't recognise that even after discussing on this sort 
of an important topic. It's a shame, I must say. Sir, in the 21" century, it is a 
shame that in a civilised country like ours which boasts of civilisation, the history 
of civilisation with pride that we have a civilisation of thousands of years, but 
unfortunately, in our country people die out of sheer frustration because of 
pauperisation. Sir, I am sure that my erudit colleagues who are economists by 
vocation or by profession, they will appreciate that we are in a transition. I find it 
extremely difficult in which slot India should be put, whether it is a developed 
nation or it is a developing nation or yet to be developed nation or under-developed 
nation, I really find it very difficult because looking at the upper strata or the 
creamy layer of the society, creamy layer of the country, I find it is a

on this problem of suicides of farmers in the country with a great sadness,

pride. If we look at the way they have been able to improve our food 
production, we are very proud of our farmers. But it is an unfortunate 
occasion that this House has to diliberate on this serious issue with sadness. 
I have been listening to my senior colleagues for the past two-and-a-half 
hours. I agree with the suggestions, the analyses and the remedial 
measures suggested. Sir, I would also like to add a few points. 
Sir, this process of suicide is more of a psychological process. It is 
also a sociological process and it is an economical process. This is a 
combination of all these processes. It is not an event occurring at one 
place, in one village or in one State. There are a series of unfortunate 
suicide deaths. It is a process which has started, as pointed out rightly by 
my colleague and my close friend, Mr. Madhu, Sir, in the last decade. For 
the last ten years we have been experiencing this problem, but it has 
touched the nerves of this country's policy-makers only after it crosses 
the figure of 10,000. It is very unfortunate. Sir. I am sorry to say this, at 
least we are able to come to a point and we are now deciding and 
deliberating on how to stop this unfortunate process. Sir, I would like to 
also say that it is not the farmers alone who are the sufferes, but those 
who are dependent on the farmers are also the worst sufferers, the 
agricultural labourers. If the farmers is happy, the people dependent on 
him, the agricultural labourers, who also constitute a majority in the rural 
villages, are happy too. Most of them are poor. Most of the poor depend on 
the farmers because that is how their harmonious life goes on in the villages. 
Once the farmer is in a state of despair, the whole chain of events will 
affect the others also. In that way, we should take it much more seriously 
because it has remifications in the other fields of activity. Sir, you know, it 
is an accepted fact, not only in our country but the world over, that agriculture 
is not economically viable because if you look 30 years back, even in the 
developed countries, 60-70 per cent of them used to do agriculture. But 
later on, this shift has come, 6-7 per cent; world over we find this shift from 
agriculture to the industrial business etc. Similarly, Sir, here also, we 
know that it is not economical, but 70 per cent of our population lives in 
the villages. We do not have any other alternative. We are forced to stick 
on to agriculture. Sir, the farmers, as you know,—I am talking about the 
average farmer with 2-3 acres or one acre or one-and-a-half acres of land 
who is a very simple person works very hard. Not only he but the entire
